flawed_step: Step 3: the claim that every stable matching must equal the man-optimal matching M0 does not hold. The Gale–Shapley theory only shows that each man does at least as well in M0 as in any stable matching. It does not show that there is only one stable matching.
counterexample: n=2. Men's preferences: m1: w1 > w2; m2: w2 > w1. Women's preferences: w1: m2 > m1; w2: m1 > m2. Matching A = {(m1,w1),(m2,w2)} is stable because each man has his first choice, so no man wants to switch. Matching B = {(m1,w2),(m2,w1)} is stable because each woman has her first choice, so no woman wants to switch. A and B are different.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt:
1. Let M0 be the matching produced by men-proposing Gale–Shapley. Justified: the algorithm always ends in a stable matching, so at least one exists.
2. Every man is matched in M0 to the best partner he has in any stable matching. Justified: this is the standard man-optimality result for the proposal algorithm.
3. So any stable matching M equals M0. NOT justified: man-optimality means each man weakly prefers M0 to M. It does not mean M = M0. Other stable matchings, where men do worse and women do better, may exist.
4. So the stable matching is unique. Not justified: it depends on Step 3.
Checking the gap with the smallest case: take n=2 with m1: w1>w2, m2: w2>w1, w1: m2>m1, w2: m1>m2.
- Matching A = {m1w1, m2w2}. Each man has his top choice, so no man is in a blocking pair, so A is stable.
- Matching B = {m1w2, m2w1}. Each woman has her top choice, so no woman is in a blocking pair, so B is stable.
- A ≠ B.
So under the stated definition, stable matchings need not be unique, and the statement is false. (A stable matching always exists, but there can be more than one.)
